questions.prompt: What major performance improvement does TLS 1.3 offer over TLS 1.2 during a new handshake?
questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 combines key share generation with ClientHello/ServerHello, completing the cryptographic handshake in 1-RTT rather than 2-RTT.

questions.prompt: Why was the RSA Key Exchange deprecated in TLS 1.3?
questions.explanation: Static RSA key exchange lacked Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS): compromising the server's long-term private key enables decryption of past recorded sessions.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of the 'Client Random' and 'Server Random' nonces?
options: To prevent replay attacks and ensure unique session keys
questions.explanation: Random nonces ensure freshness across sessions, preventing replay attacks and guaranteeing independent session keys even if parameters match.

questions.prompt: In the TLS handshake, what is the role of the 'ChangeCipherSpec' message in TLS 1.2?
options: To signal that subsequent records will be encrypted
questions.explanation: ChangeCipherSpec explicitly signaled to the receiving peer that all following records would be encrypted under negotiated session keys.

questions.prompt: Which cryptographic primitive is used to derive the Master Secret in TLS 1.2?
questions.explanation: TLS 1.2 uses HMAC-based Pseudo-Random Function (PRF) with SHA-256 to expand the Pre-Master Secret and random nonces into the 48-byte Master Secret.

questions.prompt: What happens if a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) modifies the handshake messages in transit?
options: The server silently drops the client
The client sends a new ClientHello
questions.explanation: The 'Finished' message encrypts a cryptographic MAC of all previous handshake messages; any in-transit tampering causes authentication verification failure.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is typically authenticated via a Digital Certificate during the handshake?
questions.explanation: Standard one-way TLS authenticates the Server identity using an X.509 certificate signed by a recognized Certificate Authority (CA).

questions.prompt: What does Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) guarantee in modern TLS?
options: A compromised server private key won't decrypt past recorded traffic
Keys are sent in plaintext securely
The server can forward traffic perfectly
questions.explanation: PFS guarantees that ephemeral session keys (generated via ECDHE) cannot be computed retroactively even if the long-term server private key is leaked.

questions.prompt: What type of cipher is AES-128-GCM, commonly used in modern TLS?
questions.explanation: AES-GCM is an AEAD cipher, providing both symmetric confidentiality and built-in cryptographic authentication tag verification in a single primitive.

questions.prompt: Which IETF RFC specification defines the modern Transport Layer Security protocol version 1.3 (TLS 1.3)?
questions.explanation: RFC 8446 (published in August 2018) specifies TLS 1.3, superseding TLS 1.2 defined in RFC 5246.
